ref: 4.4.2 (ANF section 2; Harvey Book IV ch.4 sec.2)
greek: omnia enim mensura et ordine Deus facit, et nihil non mensum apud eum, quoniam nec incompositum. Et bene, qui dixit immensum Patrem in Filio mensuratum: mensura enim Patris Filius, quoniam et capit eum.
greek_edition: Harvey 1857 Latin (Latin, not Greek). Read from Google djvu OCR (sanctiirenaeiep00harvgoog); PDF page 164 OCR confirms 'immensum Patrem in Filio mensuratum: mensura enim Patris Filius'. OCR-level.
english: Well spoke he, who said that the unmeasurable Father was Himself subjected to measure in the Son; for the Son is the measure of the Father, since He also comprehends Him.
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1)
page: ANF printed p. 466 (PDF p. 484 of the 1913 scan); Harvey Latin printed p. 153 (PDF 164)
what_it_says: Irenaeus says the Father, unmeasurable, was subjected to measure in the Son, who is the Father's measure and comprehends him.
limits: The 'measure' is a Latin-Greek word-play (mensura); Irenaeus is speaking of the Son as the Father's measure in the sense of the Son's revealing of the Father, not of Nicene consubstantiality; the Greek is not extant here. Opponents read 'subjected to measure' as proof of a lesser Son.

ref: 4.6.6 (ANF section 6; Harvey Book IV ch.6 sec.6)
greek: Et per ipsum Verbum visibilem et palpabilem factum, Pater ostendebatur, etiamsi non omnes similiter credebant ei; sed omnes viderunt in Filio Patrem: invisibile etenim Filii Pater, visibile autem Patris Filius.
greek_edition: Harvey 1857 Latin (Google djvu OCR; PDF p.172 OCR shows 'etenim Filii Pater, visibile autem Patris Filius'). 'invisibile' + 'etenim' join is OCR-inferred (line break). Harvey's footnote 8 gives Greek 'τὸ ἀόρατον γὰρ τοῦ Υἱοῦ Πατὴρ, τὸ δὲ ὁρατὸν τοῦ Πατρὸς Υἱός' as his own note (not a surviving Greek witness).
english: And through the Word Himself who had been made visible and palpable, was the Father shown forth, although all did not equally believe in Him; but all saw the Father in the Son: for the Father is the invisible of the Son, but the Son the visible of the Father.
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1)
page: ANF printed p. 469 (PDF 487); Harvey Latin printed p. 161 (PDF 172)
what_it_says: The Father is seen in the Son: the Father is invisible in relation to the Son, and the Son is the visible of the Father.
limits: Irenaeus's phrase is about revelation (the Son makes the invisible Father known) and says nothing about the Son's essence or equality; an Arian can read 'the Son the visible of the Father' as a lesser, manifested being. The sentence is the reading the Monarchian and Arian camps both quote. Greek not extant.

ref: 4.20.1 (ANF section 1; Harvey Book IV ch.20 sec.1)
greek: Nec enim indigebat horum Deus ad faciendum quae ipse apud se praefinierat fieri, quasi ipse suas non haberet manus. Adest enim ei semper Verbum et Sapientia, Filius et Spiritus, per quos, et in quibus omnia libere et sponte fecit.
greek_edition: Harvey 1857 Latin (Google djvu OCR; PDF p.224 OCR 'quasi ipse suas non haberet manus. Adest enim ei semper Verbum et Sapientia, Filius et Spiritus'). OCR-level spelling.
english: For with Him were always present the Word and Wisdom, the Son and the Spirit, by whom and in whom, freely and spontaneously, He made all things; ... For God did not stand in need of these [beings], ... as if He did not possess His own hands.
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1)
page: ANF printed p. 487 (PDF 505); Harvey Latin printed p. 213 (PDF 224)
what_it_says: God made all things with the Word and Wisdom, namely the Son and the Spirit, always present with Him, and needs no angels as hands.
limits: 'Word and Wisdom' are in apposition to 'Son and Spirit' here, but Irenaeus does not say the Spirit is a person distinct in the Nicene sense; the literal phrase 'two hands' is not in this section (ANF Book V, printed p. 546 / PDF 564 has the 'two hands' wording, not read cleanly). Greek not extant.

ref: 4.20.3 (ANF section 3; Harvey Book IV ch.20 sec.3)
greek: Et quoniam Verbum, id est Filius, semper cum Patre erat, per multa demonstravimus. Quoniam autem et Sapientia, quae est Spiritus, erat apud eum ante omnem constitutionem, per Salomonem ait: Deus sapientia fundavit terram.
greek_edition: Harvey 1857 Latin (Google djvu OCR; PDF p.225 OCR confirms 'Quoniam autem et Sapientia, quae est Spiritus'). OCR-level.
english: I have also largely demonstrated, that the Word, namely the Son, was always with the Father; and that Wisdom also, which is the Spirit, was present with Him, anterior to all creation.
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1)
page: ANF printed p. 488 (PDF 506); Harvey Latin printed p. 214 (PDF 225)
what_it_says: Irenaeus identifies the Word with the Son and Wisdom (Prov 8) with the Spirit, both present with the Father before creation.
limits: This identification (Wisdom = Spirit) is Irenaeus's own and differs from Justin (Dial. 61) and Tertullian who read Wisdom as the Son; so the Prov 8 'Wisdom' passage is not a clean proof of a Nicene Trinity. Latin 'Sapientia' has no surviving Greek here.

ref: 2.28.6 (ANF section 6; Harvey Book II ch.28 sec.6)
english: But of that day and that hour knows no man, neither the Son, but the Father only. If, then, the Son was not ashamed to ascribe the knowledge of that day to the Father only, ... Since therefore His generation is unspeakable, those who strive to set forth generations and productions cannot be in their right mind.
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1)
what_it_says: Irenaeus quotes the Son's ignorance of the day and hour (Mark 13:32) and argues that if the Son left that to the Father, Christians should leave deeper questions, including the Son's generation, to God.
limits: ANF gives no scripture reference at the quotation (Mark 13:32 identified by me from the words). Irenaeus does not explain the ignorance as the Son's human knowledge; the answer is a rule of humility, not a Nicene exegesis, and does not cover the 'Son does not know' in Mark's sense. Latin of this section not read in this pass.

ref: 2.28.5 (ANF section 5; Harvey Book II ch.28 sec.5)
english: But God being all Mind, and all Logos, both speaks exactly what He thinks, and thinks exactly what He speaks. For His thought is Logos, and Logos is Mind, and Mind comprehending all things is the Father Himself.
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1)
what_it_says: God is all Mind and all Logos; Logos is not a third thing produced after God, and Logos and Mind are the Father himself.
limits: Irenaeus rejects Logos as a third-place product but does not use 'hypostasis' or 'consubstantial' language; the Son is not named in this sentence, so the link to the Son is by context. Latin/Greek not read.

english: When then was God without that which is proper to Him? Or how can a man consider that which is proper, as foreign and alien in essence?
translator: John Henry Newman and Archibald Robertson (NPNF2 vol. 4)
edition: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 4 (text read on newadvent, page numbers not shown)
what_it_says: The Son is proper to the Father's essence, so the Father was never without him; the Son is not foreign to the Father in essence.
limits: Athanasius argues against Arians that the Son is eternally from the Father's essence; it answers the 'when the Son was not' objection to the Son as measure/visible of the Father (Haer. 4.4.2, 4.6.6), but does not discuss Irenaeus's 'Son is measure' language. Greek not read.

ref: Athanasius, Orationes contra Arianos 3.45 (NPNF2 sec. 45; the Mark 13:32 discussion is secs. 42-49)
english: ...let us, who love Christ and bear Christ within us, know that the Word, not as ignorant, considered as Word, has said 'I know not,' for He knows, but as showing His manhood, in that to be ignorant is proper to man...
translator: John Henry Newman and Archibald Robertson (NPNF2 vol. 4)
edition: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 4 (text read on newadvent)
what_it_says: The Word speaks 'I know not' as man, not as Word, since to be ignorant is proper to a human being; the Son knows the day as God.
limits: This is the 'as man' reading of Mark 13:32 (the Son's human knowledge). Irenaeus gives no such explanation; he gives a rule of humility (2.28.6). Athanasius's 'as man' reading is not one Irenaeus's Latin supports. Greek not read.

ref: Thomas Aquinas, Summa theologiae I q.42 a.5 (Son in the Father, and conversely)
english: The Father is in the Son by His essence, forasmuch as the Father is His own essence, and communicates His essence to the Son not by any change on His part... since the Son is His own essence, it follows that He Himself is in the Father in Whom is His essence.
translator: Fathers of the English Dominican Province (as credited on newadvent)
edition: Summa theologiae I q.42 (newadvent summa/1042.htm); the brief's 'a.4' is article 4 on equality, the mutual indwelling is article 5
what_it_says: The Father and Son are in each other by essence, relation and origin, and the Son is his own essence, so the Son is in the Father.
limits: Thirteenth-century scholastic metaphysics, not Irenaeus; it answers the 'Father greater' and separation questions but uses 'essence' and 'relation' vocabulary Irenaeus lacks. Latin not read.

ref: Thomas Aquinas, Summa theologiae III q.10 a.2 ad 1 (Christ's knowledge; Mark 13:32)
english: He is said, therefore, not to know the day and the hour of the Judgment, for that He does not make it known... But the Father is said to know, because He imparted this knowledge to the Son. Hence, by saying but the Father, we are given to understand that the Son knows, not merely in the Divine Nature, but also in the human.
translator: Fathers of the English Dominican Province (as credited on newadvent)
what_it_says: The Son is said not to know the day because he does not reveal it; the Son knows it in both natures.
limits: Aquinas's 'does not make it known' reading is the one Irenaeus's 'the Son did not so know as to show his disciples' resembles; Aquinas adds Christ's human knowledge, which Irenaeus does not. Latin not read.

ref: Augustine, De Trinitate I.12 (Chapter 12, Mark 13:32; paragraph number not shown in newadvent text)
english: Again, Of that day and that hour knows no man, no, not the angels which are in heaven; neither the Son, but the Father. For He is ignorant of this, as making others ignorant; that is, in that He did not so know as at that time to show His disciples.
edition: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series, vol. 3 (newadvent fathers/130101.htm; page numbers not shown)
what_it_says: The Son is ignorant of the day 'as making others ignorant': he did not reveal it to the disciples at that time.
limits: Same 'not revealed' reading as Irenaeus's 2.28.6 and Aquinas; Augustine also says the Son knows as the Word. Latin not read in this pass (Latin via PL 42 not opened).

ref: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oratio 29 (Third Theological Oration) sec. 8
english: How then was He begotten? This Generation would have been no great thing, if you could have comprehended it... And do not even then venture to speculate on the Generation of God; for that would be unsafe. For even if you knew all about your own, yet you do not by any means know about God's.
translator: Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow (NPNF2 vol. 7)
edition: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 7 (newadvent fathers/310229.htm)
what_it_says: The Son's generation cannot be comprehended, so one should not speculate about it.
limits: Gregory's 'Generation' argument closely parallels Irenaeus 2.28.6 (no one knows how the Son was produced); Gregory is later (c.380) and uses 'Generation' as a term with Nicene content. Greek not read.

ref: Justin, Dialogus cum Tryphone 61 (Wisdom begotten of the Father)
english: ...since He ministers to the Father's will, and since He was begotten of the Father by an act of will; just as we see happening among ourselves: for when we give out some word, we beget the word; yet not by abscission... The Word of Wisdom, who is Himself this God begotten of the Father of all things, and Word, and Wisdom, and Power, and the Glory of the Begetter.
translator: Marcus Dods and George Reith (ANF vol. 1)
page: ANF printed p. 227 (PDF 245; the running head OCRs as '22' with an apostrophe, read as 227)
what_it_says: The Word/Wisdom is begotten of the Father by an act of will, as fire from fire, and is himself God.
limits: Justin identifies Wisdom with the Son, not the Spirit as Irenaeus does in 4.20.3; the 'begotten by an act of will' wording was read by later Arians as subordinate, and Justin has no Nicene homoousios. Greek not read.

english: ...when I asserted that this power was begotten from the Father, by His power and will, but not by abscission, as if the essence of the Father were divided.
translator: Marcus Dods and George Reith (ANF vol. 1)
what_it_says: The Word/Power is begotten from the Father without the Father's essence being divided.
limits: Justin's 'by His power and will' is an Arian-sounding formula; the 'not by abscission' answers the separation worry but does not give the Nicene sameness of essence. Greek not read.

english: But the Son of God is the Logos of the Father, in idea and in operation; for after the pattern of Him and by Him were all things made, the Father and the Son being one. And, the Son being in the Father and the Father in the Son, in oneness and power of spirit, the understanding and reason of the Father is the Son of God.
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (newadvent fathers/0205.htm; page numbers not shown)
what_it_says: The Son is the Father's Logos in idea and operation; the Father and Son are one, each in the other.
limits: Athenagoras's Logos-Son is a 'first product' ('not as having been brought into existence'), a formula later judged subordinationist; the Greek 'νοῦς καὶ λόγος' appears in the newadvent HTML but no named Greek edition is given, so not used as a Greek quote.

english: Was the Word of God put forth or not? ... If He was put forth, then acknowledge that the true doctrine has a prolation; and never mind heresy, when in any point it mimics the truth.
what_it_says: Catholic teaching may use 'prolation' (proferre) for the Word, provided it is not separated from the Father as Valentinus's aeons are.
limits: Tertullian accepts prolatio where Irenaeus (2.28.5-6) rejects 'third place' production; they agree that Gnostic prolation is wrong but differ on the vocabulary. Latin of Adv. Prax. 8 not read in this pass.
